title: Global functions on a proper reduced connected algebraic space
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] and $X$ an algebraic space over $\operatorname{Spec}k$ [def-pc-scheme, def-trf-algebraic-space]. Suppose the structure morphism is proper [def-sfb-space-morphism-properties], meaning separated, of finite type and universally closed. Suppose $X$ is reduced, meaning the rings of affine etale scheme charts have no nonzero nilpotents, and $|X|$ is nonempty and connected in the atlas topology [def-a1-space-point-topology]. Then $\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)$ is a field, finite-dimensional as a $k$-algebra. Here $\mathcal O_X$ is the structure sheaf on the small etale site. No geometric reducedness or geometric connectedness is assumed.

source.place: Tag 0DMY, lemma-proper-geometrically-reduced-global-sections, clauses (1)--(3), restricted to a single nonempty connected component

proof.text: Put $A=\Gamma(X_{\mathrm{et}},\mathcal O_X)$ and let $C$ be the set of connected components of $|X|$. Apply [lem-sfb-space-proper-global-algebra-components] to the given proper algebraic space over the field $k$. It gives a finite-dimensional $k$-algebra $A$ and the restriction isomorphism $A\simeq\prod_{c\in C}\Gamma(c_{\mathrm{et}},\mathcal O_c)$. Since $X$ is reduced, every factor in this product is a finite field extension of $k$. This application uses only ordinary reducedness, not geometric reducedness.

source.place: Tag 0DMY, lemma-proper-geometrically-reduced-global-sections, clauses (1)--(3) and the component decomposition in the proof of (2)

proof.text: The whole set $|X|$ is nonempty and connected, so it is itself a maximal nonempty connected subset. Every connected component, being maximal among such subsets and contained in $|X|$, is therefore $|X|$. Thus $C$ has exactly one element $c_0$. Evaluation at $c_0$ identifies the preceding product with its sole factor (the inverse sends an element to the function on the singleton having that value). Composing with restriction gives a $k$-algebra isomorphism from $A$ to a field finite over $k$. Hence $A$ is a field and finite-dimensional over $k$, as claimed.
